newsitem.title: INDIA: India rupee dips sharply as importers, RBI buy dlr.
newsitem.headline: India rupee dips sharply as importers, RBI buy dlr.

text.p: The rupee fell sharply against the dollar on Friday as the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) took advantage of a rare rising trend in corporate demand to push down the overvalued Indian currency, dealers said.
"It is a good strategy -- hit on a day when there is good demand (for dollars)," said the chief dealer at a private bank.
"That will take the pressure off their backs for some time."
The spot rupee opened Friday steady at 35.705/710. Most of the morning transactions were at 35.72/73 as rising corporate demand for dollars, seen on Thursday, continued, dealers said.
The Industrial Development Bank of India sold dollars, leading to a mild rise in the rupee which did not last.
In a smart move, the RBI struck the market repeatedly, buying dollars in the forward market and pushing down the rupee from 35.74 level to 35.76, dealers said.
RBI purchases aggravated the corporate demand, pushing the rupee to a low of 35.82 on Friday. The rupee has been trading at 35.69/71 range in recent weeks, thanks to RBI intervention.
"It was the right move -- coming when demand is there," said the chief dealer at a state-run bank in Bombay. "This way, he can move the market with less volumes."
"When there is demand, intervention becomes meaningful and effective," said Moses Harding, chief dealer at IndusInd Bank.
Spot rupee closed Friday at 35.78/79 against the dollar.

In the recent past, the RBI had bought as much as $80 million in one day with little impact on the exchange rate, he said. The RBI has been intervening all these days against the backdrop of lack of dollar demand and abundant supplies.
On Friday, RBI's purchases are estimated at just under $40 million, bankers said. But the impact of its intervention far exceeded the small amount of its intervention, they said.
RBI bought outright dollars in October, December and January maturities, dealers said.
"It's a combination of factors -- RBI buying, import covering and some inter-bank short-covering," a dealer said.
The rupee saw a high of 35.71 and a low of 35.82 on Friday.
The impact of RBI's intervention in the forward market -- its recent intervention has been in the spot section -- pushed up premiums by nearly eight paise, dealers said.

"Premiums have not moved for one month, but rose sharply today," said a delighted dealer, saying the market had at last become interesting. The sentiment is expected to continue next week, dealers said.
The six-month annualised premium closed Friday at 3.85 percent, up from the previous 3.64 percent.
Some dealers said RBI was focusing on the forwards to help Indian exporters who have been complaining about the overvalued rupee hurting Indian competitiveness.
"But I don't see the six-month premiums going beyond the 4.0-4.5 percent range," Harding of IndusInd Bank said.
"For the past two days, importers have been covering, fearing some action at depreciating the rupee," a dealer said.
